articles.title: The Option Nobody Chooses Can Still Change Your Mind
articles.excerpt: A third option that almost nobody picks can quietly move the choice between the other two. The decoy effect explains why the middle row on a price list deserves a second look before you decide.
articles.body_html:
A price list with three rows can look reassuringly complete. One row is basic, one is generous, and one sits between them with no obvious reason to exist. It is tempting to ignore that middle row completely. Yet the row nobody chooses may still be doing quiet work: it can change how the other two rows feel.

The prices stay exactly where they were. What changes is the comparison your mind is invited to make. In economics, that invitation has a name — the decoy effect — and learning to notice it is a practical skill.

All figures in this article are in US dollars and come from the sources cited at the end.

A choice that should not matter

Start with a simple expectation. If you are choosing between two options, adding a third option should not make either of the first two more popular. At most, the new option should take some choices for itself. Economists call this expectation regularity: an existing option cannot gain simply because the menu grew.

Huber, Payne and Puto tested that expectation in 1982. In the study summarized by the American Psychological Association, 153 college students chose among a decoy, a target, and a competitor. The decoy was asymmetrically dominated: the target was clearly better than it, while the competitor was not clearly better in the same direct way. Could that weak third option raise the target’s share? It could.

What the first experiments found

The original report examined six product classes, with the target role reversed so that each class produced two cases — twelve cases in all. In 10 of those 12 cases, regularity was violated in the expected direction: adding the decoy increased the probability of choosing the target. Across the cases, the overall gain in the target’s choice probability was 7 percentage points.

MeasureResultWhy it matters
Cases moving in the expected direction10 of 12The effect was not confined to one product class
Overall gain for the target7 percentage pointsA modest shift can still decide many close choices
Choices of the decoy itselfAbout 2%People recognized the decoy as weak, yet it still influenced the set

The last line matters. Huber, Payne and Puto later noted that the decoy’s average choice proportion was limited to approximately 2%, indicating that dominance was recognized. Participants were not mainly fooled into buying the weak option; it changed the contest between the stronger ones.

The subscription demonstration

The clearest illustration is a subscription demonstration reported by Dan Ariely and reproduced in later economics writing. Three annual offers were shown: web access only for $59, print only for $125, and print plus web access for $125. The print-only offer is the decoy, because the combined offer gives more for the same $125.

Choice setWeb only ($59)Print only ($125)Print + web ($125)
Three offers shown16%0%84%
Print-only offer removed68%Not offered32%

Removing an offer chosen by nobody changed the majority. The combined offer rose from 32% without the decoy to 84% with it — a shift of 52 percentage points. The upgrade costs $66. Treated as 100 purchases, the reported choices imply revenue of $11,444 with the decoy and $8,012 without it: a $3,432 difference, or 52 extra combined-offer choices multiplied by $66. That is arithmetic from reported choices, not evidence about real sales, but it shows how a comparison can move money.

Why an easy comparison feels like a reason

The mechanism is comparison. Between target and decoy, there is no difficult trade-off: the combined offer contains the print-only offer and adds web access at the same price. Between target and competitor, the trade-off is real: pay $66 more, or keep the lower price and give up print. The decoy offers one easy victory first, and that victory can make the harder decision feel settled.

Huber, Payne and Puto made the same distinction in 2014: competitor-versus-decoy still requires trade-offs, while target-versus-decoy does not. The lesson is not that people are careless. A clear comparison is attractive, especially when the underlying preference is weak.

When the effect weakens

The decoy effect is real, but it is not unlimited. The same 2014 review identifies conditions that inhibit it: strong prior trade-offs, difficulty in identifying the dominance relationship quickly, wide differences in what people value, and a strong liking or disliking for the decoy itself. It also notes that the effect is weaker, and sometimes reversed, with rich nonnumeric stimuli.

That boundary is useful. If you know you never use print, the $66 upgrade has little to recommend it. If you are uncertain and meet the choice as three neat rows of numbers, context has more room to work. The response is not suspicion; it is structure.

What to do before you choose

Use the menu, but do not let the menu finish the reasoning for you. Five steps restore the decision to your own needs.

  1. Remove the dominated row mentally. If one option gives less for the same or a higher price, cross it out and compare only the options you would genuinely choose.
  2. Price the upgrade on its own. Ask whether the extra feature is worth $66 by itself, not whether it looks generous beside a weaker row.
  3. Write your rule before the tiers. Decide the budget, the frequency of use, and the feature you actually need before reading the labels.
  4. Compare totals, not adjectives. Convert monthly, annual, and introductory prices into the same period and the same unit before judging value.
  5. Let a pause do quiet work. For non-urgent purchases, return later with the two surviving options only. A preference that survives the pause is more likely to be yours.

These steps convert a designed menu back into a personal decision. The middle row may still inform you, but it no longer casts the deciding vote.

So here is the question to carry into the next price list: if the option nobody chooses disappeared, would your choice remain the same — and if not, which comparison was really deciding for you?

Key takeaways

  • The decoy effect occurs when adding an asymmetrically dominated option increases the share of the option that dominates it.
  • Huber, Payne and Puto’s 1982 study used 153 college students choosing among a decoy, a target, and a competitor.
  • In the original report, regularity moved in the expected direction in 10 of 12 cases, with an overall target gain of 7 percentage points.
  • The decoy itself was chosen only about 2% of the time in the original studies, so recognition did not remove its influence.
  • In Ariely’s reported subscription demonstration, the combined offer rose from 32% without the print-only decoy to 84% with it.
  • Before choosing, remove dominated rows, price the upgrade alone, and compare totals over the same period.

Sources

  • Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (1982). Adding asymmetrically dominated alternatives: Violations of regularity and the similarity hypothesis. Journal of Consumer Research, 9(1), 90–98 — doi.org
  • Huber, J., Payne, J. W., & Puto, C. (2014). Let’s be honest about the attraction effect. Journal of Marketing Research, 51(4), 520–525 — article PDF
  • Herweg, F., Müller, D., & Weinschenk, P. (2016). Salience, competition, and decoy goods. CESifo Working Paper No. 6168, reproducing Ariely’s subscription example and reported choices — cesifo.org

Note: the 153-student description and the definition of asymmetric dominance come from Huber, Payne and Puto (1982); the 10-of-12 and 7-percentage-point figures come from the same study’s reported Exhibit 3; the approximately 2% decoy choice proportion and the boundary conditions come from Huber, Payne and Puto (2014). The subscription percentages are Ariely’s reported demonstration as reproduced by Herweg, Müller and Weinschenk (2016). The $66 upgrade, 52-percentage-point shift, $11,444 and $8,012 totals, and $3,432 difference are arithmetic worked from those stated figures and verified by calculation.

articles.title: One Wrong Digit Can Stop a Transfer: How Your IBAN Checks Itself
articles.excerpt: Two digits inside every IBAN exist for one purpose: to check all the others. The MOD-97 calculation behind them catches a single wrong digit or swapped pair before money moves — here is how it works, and what it cannot do.
articles.body_html:
You type a long account number into a transfer form, press continue, and the bank refuses it: the account number is invalid. Nothing has been sent or lost, yet the message feels like an obstacle. It is worth seeing differently: that refusal is a small act of protection, performed by the number itself.

An International Bank Account Number, or IBAN, is an address with a built-in proofreader: two of its characters exist only to check all the others. Understanding them is a practical skill, because transfers matter most precisely when careful typing is hardest.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

An address with a built-in proofreader

The IBAN is defined by the international standard ISO 13616, and SWIFT acts as its registration authority, publishing the official format for each country in the IBAN Registry. The registry lists 89 countries and territories. Every IBAN, wherever it is issued, has the same three parts:

PartLengthWhat it tells the bank
Country code2 lettersThe country where the account is held
Check digits2 digitsA checksum calculated from every other character
Basic Bank Account Number (BBAN)Up to 30 charactersThe domestic bank identifier and account number, in a format fixed for that country

The whole IBAN may run to 34 characters, but within any one country the length never varies: 15 characters in Norway, 22 in Germany and the United Kingdom, 27 in France, and 31 in Malta. On paper, IBANs are printed in groups of four for easier reading; electronically, the spaces are removed. The fixed length is itself a first check — a number one character short is wrong before any arithmetic begins.

The two digits that check all the others

The check digits are calculated by the MOD 97-10 method of ISO/IEC 7064, the standard for check character systems that protect copied and keyed data against error. Validation follows four steps:

  1. Move the first four characters — the country code and check digits — to the end of the string.
  2. Replace every letter with a number: A becomes 10, B becomes 11, and so on to Z, which becomes 35.
  3. Divide the resulting number, treated as one very large integer, by 97.
  4. Compare the remainder. A correctly formed IBAN leaves a remainder of exactly 1. Any other remainder means at least one character is wrong.

ISO/IEC 7064 is designed to detect all single substitution errors — one character replaced by another — and all or nearly all transpositions, in which two characters change places. The check digits are generated in the range 02 to 98. The choice of 97 is deliberate: it is prime, and a remainder modulo 97 can take 97 possible values, so a random corruption has only about one chance in 97 of still producing the required remainder of 1.

Watch it work: one correct number, two typos

Take the specimen German IBAN from the registry examples, DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 00 — 22 characters, the fixed German length:

StepResult
Move DE89 to the end370400440532013000DE89
Replace letters (D = 13, E = 14)370400440532013000131489
Divide by 97Remainder 1 — the IBAN is correctly formed

Now introduce the two most common typing mistakes. Change the final digit from 0 to 1, and the remainder becomes 28: rejected. Swap the neighbouring digits 37 to 73, and the remainder also becomes 28: rejected. Either slip is caught before any money moves.

VersionRemainder after division by 97Result
Correct IBAN1Accepted as correctly formed
One digit changed (final 0 typed as 1)28Rejected
Two neighbouring digits swapped (37 typed as 73)28Rejected

The arithmetic is simple. Changing one digit changes the large number by a multiple of a power of ten; because 97 is prime and divides neither that power of ten nor the difference between two digits, the remainder must change. The same holds for a swap of neighbouring digits. For digit-for-digit errors, the check catches every one.

What the check cannot do

A remainder of 1 proves only that the IBAN is correctly formed. It does not prove that the account exists, is open, or belongs to the person you intend to pay. Copy a complete, valid IBAN belonging to someone else, and the arithmetic will approve it without hesitation.

The same limit applies to fraud. If payment instructions arrive with an altered IBAN — a familiar invoice carrying an unfamiliar account number — the checksum will pass, because the substituted number is itself correctly formed. The check digits guard against typing accidents, not deception; confirming that changed details genuinely come from the intended recipient is a separate step no arithmetic can perform. Several errors made together could also, in principle, cancel out and still leave a remainder of 1 — the one-in-97 figure measures that residual risk.

What to do before you press send

The check digits do their work automatically, but five habits let them work at their best.

  1. Copy electronically where you can. A pasted IBAN cannot contain a typing error. Reserve manual entry for occasions when no electronic copy exists.
  2. Read in groups of four. Compare the IBAN group by group against the source, exactly as printed. Most errors hide in the middle groups, where attention fades.
  3. Treat a rejection as information. Look first for one wrong digit or one swapped pair — the errors the check is built to find. Never alter digits at random until the form accepts the number; a forced number may be correctly formed and still wrong.
  4. Verify changed details through a known channel. Confirm new payment details using contact information you already trust, not information supplied in the same message.
  5. Check the confirmation screen as a whole. Read the recipient name, the IBAN, and the amount together. The checksum verified the number; only you can verify it is the right one.

These habits take less than a minute, and they make a long, fragile string of characters what it was designed to be: a number that arrives intact, or not at all.

So here is the question to carry into your next transfer: when a form rejects an account number you have typed, will you treat the refusal as an obstacle — or as the two hardest-working digits in banking, doing exactly the job they were given?

Key takeaways

  • An IBAN (ISO 13616) has three parts: a two-letter country code, two check digits, and a Basic Bank Account Number of up to 30 characters — 34 characters at most, with a fixed length in each country.
  • SWIFT, the registration authority for ISO 13616, publishes each national format in the IBAN Registry, which lists 89 countries and territories; lengths run from 15 characters in Norway to 31 in Malta.
  • Validation uses ISO/IEC 7064 MOD 97-10: move the first four characters to the end, replace letters with numbers (A = 10 to Z = 35), divide by 97, and require a remainder of exactly 1.
  • The method is designed to detect all single substitution errors and all or nearly all transpositions; in the worked example, one changed digit and one swapped pair each moved the remainder from 1 to 28.
  • A random corruption has only about one chance in 97 of still producing a remainder of 1.
  • A valid checksum proves correct formation only — not that the account exists or belongs to the intended recipient. Verify changed payment details through a channel you already trust.

Sources

  • SWIFT, IBAN Registry — the register of all ISO 13616-compliant national IBAN formats, including structure, fixed length per country, and specimen IBANs — swift.com
  • ISO, “Banking on safe transactions” — on ISO 13616, the IBAN standard, and SWIFT’s role as Registration Authority — iso.org
  • ISO/IEC 7064:2003, MOD 97-10 check character system, as reproduced with the alphabetic-to-numeric conversion table (A = 10 to Z = 35) by the Federal Reserve — federalreserve.gov
  • SWIFT, Standards resources — IBAN Registry releases and registration procedures — swift.com

Note: the structural figures come from the sources cited above. The worked example is arithmetic, verified by calculation: 370400440532013000131489 divided by 97 leaves a remainder of 1; changing the final digit to 1, or swapping 37 to 73, leaves a remainder of 28 in each case. The one-in-97 figure follows from the 97 possible remainders, of which only one is accepted.

articles.title: Five Positives for Every Negative: The Ratio Behind Strong Teams
articles.excerpt: Research on couples and on 60 business teams points to the same pattern: strong relationships and strong teams produce roughly five positive interactions for every negative one. The number is not magic — but the direction is worth following.
articles.body_html:
Two meetings. The same people, the same agenda, the same difficult problem on the table. In the first room, a correction lands and the discussion opens up: people ask questions, build on each other’s ideas, and leave with more energy than they brought. In the second room, the same correction lands and the air changes: answers shorten, eyes drop, and everyone leaves a little smaller.

The difference is rarely intelligence, and rarely the problem on the table. It is the balance of the conversation — how much of it builds people up, and how much knocks them down. Research from two very different worlds, marriage and business teams, points to the same surprising number.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

A ratio first seen in a marriage

Beginning in the 1970s, the psychologist John Gottman and his colleague Robert Levenson ran longitudinal studies of couples. They asked each couple to spend fifteen minutes discussing a conflict in their relationship, recorded what happened, and then followed up nine years later. From those fifteen minutes, they could predict which couples would stay together and which would divorce with over 90% accuracy, according to the Gottman Institute’s summary of the research.

The strongest signal was balance. In stable, happy marriages, positive interactions during conflict outnumbered negative ones by about five to one; at one-to-one or below, the relationship was in danger. Negativity carries unusual weight — one dismissive moment takes several positive moments to repair. Five is not a compliment quota; it measures the goodwill a relationship carries into its hardest conversations.

The same pattern in 60 business teams

Does a marriage finding say anything about work? In 2004, Marcial Losada and Emily Heaphy coded the verbal communication of 60 strategic business management teams in the American Behavioral Scientist, classifying every statement by positivity versus negativity, inquiry versus advocacy, and focus on others versus self. Grouped by performance, the teams’ positivity-to-negativity ratios differed strikingly:

Team performancePositivity-to-negativity ratioIn plain words
High5.6 to 1Nearly six positive statements for every negative one
Medium1.9 to 1Almost two positives for every negative
Low0.36 to 1About 2.8 negatives for every positive

The gap is wide: the high-performing ratio (5.614 in the study’s data) was more than fifteen times the low-performing one (0.363). High-performing teams also balanced asking questions with stating views, and attention to others with their own concerns. Positivity here is not cheerfulness; it is people feeling heard often enough to keep contributing.

Recognition is rarer than leaders think

Are such interactions common? Gallup’s analysis says only one in three workers in the United States strongly agree they received recognition or praise for good work in the past seven days — and employees who feel inadequately recognized are twice as likely to say they will quit within a year.

Asked who gave their most meaningful recognition, employees named their manager most often (28%). Gallup recommends recognition roughly every seven days, and describes the most effective kind as honest, authentic and individualised. The leader is thus the most memorable source of the interactions the ratio counts — yet in any given week, most employees receive none.

A compass, not a law of nature

Honesty requires a caution. In 2013, Nicholas Brown, Alan Sokal and Harris Friedman concluded in the American Psychologist that the claimed critical minimum ratio of 2.9013 was entirely unfounded: equations borrowed from fluid dynamics did not validly describe human emotions. Later researchers questioned the exact thresholds derived from these ratios.

That caution improves the lesson. Treat five-to-one as a compass, not a scoreboard: never manufacture praise to hit a decimal, and never swallow an honest correction to protect a ratio. The durable finding is directional — teams flourish when positives strongly outnumber negatives. Aim for a healthy surplus, and let the exact number go.

The same 36 comments, three different rooms

Imagine a one-hour meeting in which 36 comments are made. The number of comments never changes; only their balance does:

RoomPositiveNegativeRatio
The strong room3065.0 to 1
The even room18181.0 to 1
The struggling room9270.33 to 1

All three rooms talked the same amount. The strong room still had six negative moments — the ratio is five to one, not five to zero. What changed was everything around them: genuine agreement, thanks, interested questions, quick repairs. Inside that surplus, a correction is heard as information; in the struggling room, as a verdict.

What to do this week

The ratio is built from small, repeatable moves. Six are worth practising.

  1. Count one meeting. Quietly tally positives (agreement, thanks, genuine questions) against negatives (dismissal, sarcasm, personal criticism). Most leaders are surprised by their own number.
  2. Make recognition specific. Name the behaviour and its effect: not “good work,” but “your summary caught the risk early and saved us a week of rework.” Specific praise is believable; generic praise is noise.
  3. Keep a seven-day rhythm. For a team of eight, that is eight brief, honest acknowledgements a week — minutes of attention, given while the work is fresh.
  4. Separate the work from the person. Describe what you observed, explain its effect, offer a path forward. Criticism of a person closes ears; information about work opens them.
  5. Ask before you advocate. One genuine question — “what are we missing?” — often adds more than three statements of your own view.
  6. Repair quickly. Acknowledge a comment that landed badly, and apologise where due. Repair is itself a positive interaction — and the one most fully in your control.

None of this softens standards. The strong room corrected its mistakes; it simply refused to make correction its only language. Honest, specific praise is not flattery. It is fuel — the surplus of trust that lets hard truths be heard.

So here is the question to carry into your next meeting: if someone counted the balance of your team’s conversation this week, what would the ratio be — and what is one genuine positive interaction you could add today?

Key takeaways

  • Gottman and Levenson’s longitudinal studies: from a fifteen-minute conflict discussion, couples’ outcomes nine years later could be predicted with over 90% accuracy; stable marriages averaged about five positive interactions per negative one during conflict.
  • Losada and Heaphy (2004) coded 60 business teams: high-performing teams averaged a positivity-to-negativity ratio of 5.6 to 1, medium teams 1.9 to 1, and low-performing teams 0.36 to 1.
  • Gallup: only one in three U.S. workers strongly agree they received recognition in the past seven days; employees who feel inadequately recognized are twice as likely to say they will quit within a year.
  • Brown, Sokal and Friedman (2013) concluded the claimed critical positivity ratio of 2.9013 was entirely unfounded — treat five-to-one as a compass, not an exact law.
  • Positives are wider than praise: agreement, interest, questions, thanks and repair all count; a respectful correction of work need not be a negative interaction.
  • The ratio is five to one, not five to zero: strong teams still correct mistakes — inside a surplus of trust.

Sources

  • The Gottman Institute, “The Magic Relationship Ratio, According to Science” — gottman.com
  • Losada M., Heaphy E., “The Role of Positivity and Connectivity in the Performance of Business Teams: A Nonlinear Dynamics Model,” American Behavioral Scientist, 2004;47(6):740–765 — doi.org/10.1177/0002764203260208
  • Gallup, “The Importance of Employee Recognition: Low Cost, High Impact,” updated 12 January 2024 — gallup.com
  • Brown N. J. L., Sokal A. D., Friedman H. L., “The Complex Dynamics of Wishful Thinking: The Critical Positivity Ratio,” American Psychologist, 2013;68(9):801–813 — pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23855896

Note: the research figures come from the sources cited above. The meeting example is arithmetic: 30 positive and 6 negative comments give a ratio of 5.0 to 1; 18 and 18 give 1.0 to 1; 9 and 27 give 0.33 to 1.

articles.title: The Marshmallow Test: Why Waiting Is the Most Valuable Skill
articles.excerpt: In the early 1970s, a Stanford psychologist offered four-year-olds one marshmallow now, or two if they could wait fifteen minutes. The children who waited scored, on average, 210 points higher on their SATs — and the real lesson is not about willpower at all.
articles.body_html:
A small room. A low table. A four-year-old child, alone, with one marshmallow on a plate. No toys, no books, no distraction. A researcher has just left with a simple offer: eat this marshmallow now, or wait until I come back — about fifteen minutes — and you can have two.

It is one of psychology’s most famous experiments, and it began with a question that has nothing to do with marshmallows: why can some people wait for a better outcome while others take whatever is in front of them? Almost every adult decision — saving instead of spending, studying instead of scrolling — is the same choice in a different room.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

The experiment

In the late 1960s and early 1970s, the psychologist Walter Mischel ran a series of studies at Stanford’s Bing Nursery School with children aged three to five. The setup was simple: one treat now, or two after waiting alone for up to fifteen minutes. The researcher left, and the child had to decide — minute by minute — whether the second marshmallow was worth the wait.

About a third waited the full fifteen minutes; the rest gave in along the way, some within seconds. What made the study remarkable was what the waiting children did. They covered their eyes, sang to themselves, kicked the desk, turned away from the plate, and pretended the marshmallow was a picture in a frame rather than food. The children who waited longest were not the ones with the most willpower; they were the ones who found a way to make the wait easier. Waiting, it turns out, is not a fixed trait. It is a set of moves — and moves can be learned.

The 210-point surprise

The experiment became famous twenty years later, when Mischel’s team tracked the children down as teenagers. In a follow-up published in 1990 by Shoda, Mischel and Peake, they compared the school results of the children who had waited longest with those who had given in fastest — and the gap was startling.

The full fifteen-minute waiters scored, on average, 210 points higher on the SAT — the American university entrance test — than those who had waited less than thirty seconds:

SAT sectionUnder 30 secondsFull 15 minutes
Verbal524610
Mathematics528652
Combined total1,0521,262
Difference210 points

To put 210 points in context: it is roughly the size of the average SAT gap between children from advantaged and disadvantaged backgrounds. A single observation of a four-year-old predicted later test scores better than the IQ tests given to those same children at the same age.

It was never only about willpower

A finding this dramatic was bound to be re-examined. In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan repeated the experiment with a much larger and more diverse group — 918 children, rather than the small, mostly affluent group at a university nursery school — and followed them to age fifteen. The link between waiting and later test scores was still there, but it shrank by roughly two-thirds once family income, the mother’s education and the home environment were counted.

That is not a failure of the original study; it is a correction to how it was read. The ability to wait is real, and it matters — but it grows in soil. A child who has learned that promises are kept has good reason to wait; one who has learned that promised rewards often never arrive has good reason not to.

A second study proved the point. In 2013, Celeste Kidd and her colleagues at the University of Rochester gave 28 children aged three to five a small art task before the marshmallow test. Half were promised better art supplies if they waited, and the researcher came back with them; the other half were promised the same, and the researcher came back empty-handed.

Children who had just met a reliable adult waited an average of 12 minutes and 2 seconds; those who had just met an unreliable one waited 3 minutes and 2 seconds — four times less. Nine of fourteen in the reliable group waited the full fifteen minutes; in the unreliable group, one did. They were not failing a test of character; they were judging rationally. Waiting is only sensible when the person who promised the second marshmallow can be trusted to return with it. The test measures two things: the skill of waiting, and the wisdom of trusting.

The marshmallow test for adults

Adults do not sit alone in rooms with marshmallows. They sit in front of shopping apps and one-click checkouts — and the choice is the same: one pleasure now, or a larger one later. The sums are small enough to feel harmless, which is exactly why they are expensive.

Take one ordinary habit: $60 a week of impulse spending — the extra takeaway, the sale item, the gadget not on any list. That is $3,120 a year. Suppose that instead of spending it, you wait: the money is set aside and invested at an average return of 7% a year. Here is what waiting is worth:

AfterMoney set asideValue at 7% a yearGrowth from waiting
5 years$15,600$17,942$2,342
10 years$31,200$43,107$11,907
20 years$62,400$127,906$65,506

After twenty years, the money you chose not to spend has more than doubled — and more than half of it is growth, not contributions. The second marshmallow, in adult life, is compound growth: it arrives quietly, and only to people who waited. No large income is needed — only the skill those four-year-olds practised: letting a small pleasure pass, so a larger one can arrive.

How to train your waiting muscle

Fifty years of research says waiting is trainable. Self-control is less like eye colour and more like a muscle: it strengthens with use, and it has techniques. Five are worth practising.

  1. Use the ten-minute rule. When an impulse arrives, wait ten minutes. Most impulses are not decisions; they are weather, and ten minutes is usually enough for the cloud to pass.
  2. Keep a thirty-day list. Write down every non-essential purchase you want, and buy nothing on the list for thirty days. Most items will look uninteresting by then; the ones that still matter are worth buying — deliberately, without regret.
  3. Hide the marshmallow. The waiting children did best when the treat was out of sight, so remove yours: unsubscribe from sale emails, delete the shopping app, automate savings on payday. Willpower is unreliable; distance is not.
  4. Make if-then plans. Decide in advance: if I feel like buying something I did not plan, then I will close the app and check my list tomorrow. A plan made calmly is far stronger than a decision made in the moment of temptation.
  5. Keep small promises to yourself. Waiting depends on trust — including trust in yourself. Every small promise you keep makes you more reliable in your own eyes, and the next wait easier. Start with promises so small you cannot fail them.

None of this is about denying yourself pleasure. The children who waited did not go without marshmallows — they got two. Waiting is the skill that lets you enjoy more of life later, on purpose, instead of spending it all now by accident.

Next time something tempting sits in front of you — a purchase, a distraction, a shortcut — ask the question the experiment asked a four-year-old: is this the marshmallow I want, or the one I am willing to wait for?

Key takeaways

  • Mischel’s marshmallow studies (Stanford, late 1960s–early 1970s) offered children aged three to five one marshmallow now, or two after fifteen minutes; about a third waited.
  • The 1990 follow-up (Shoda, Mischel & Peake): full fifteen-minute waiters scored on average 210 points higher on the SAT than those who waited under thirty seconds (1,262 vs 1,052).
  • The 2018 replication (Watts, Duncan & Quan, 918 children) found the link shrank by roughly two-thirds once family background was counted.
  • Kidd, Palmeri & Aslin (2013): after a reliable adult, children waited 12 minutes 2 seconds on average; after an unreliable one, 3 minutes 2 seconds.
  • Waiting is trainable: the children who waited used strategies — looking away, singing, reframing.
  • $60 a week of avoided impulse spending, invested at 7%, becomes about $43,107 in ten years and $127,906 in twenty — more than half of it growth.

Sources

  • Shoda Y., Mischel W., Peake P. K., “Predicting adolescent cognitive and self-regulatory competencies from preschool delay of gratification,” Developmental Psychology, 1990;26(6):978–986 — doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.26.6.978

articles.title: Two Minutes Now, Hours Saved Later: The Rule That Clears Your Desk
articles.excerpt: A task that takes less than two minutes is not a task to schedule — it is a task to finish. David Allen’s two-minute rule, backed by research on attention and unfinished business, turns a pile of small jobs into a clear desk and a quieter mind.
articles.body_html:
Look at the small jobs waiting for you right now. The email that needs a one-line reply. The receipt that needs filing. The form that needs a signature. The message that needs a yes or a no. None of them is hard. Each one takes about two minutes. Yet they are still there — tomorrow, next week, next month.

They are small, so they feel safe to postpone. That is exactly what makes them expensive. A two-minute job deferred is not a two-minute job saved. It is a job that will cost you the doing, the remembering, and the deciding — and while it waits, it takes up a corner of your mind that you need for real work.

There is a simple rule for this, almost twenty-five years old. It comes from David Allen’s Getting Things Done, first published in 2001: if the next action on something will take less than two minutes, do it the moment it is defined. Not later today. Now.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

The rule in one sentence

Allen’s rule is not about speed. It is about a cutoff point. Writing a task down, tracking it, and deciding what to do with it a second time takes longer than two minutes — so below that line, doing it is cheaper than managing it. As Allen puts it: “If an action will take less than two minutes, it should be done at the moment it is defined.”

Two minutes is a guideline, not a law: the cutoff can stretch to five or ten minutes when you have a long stretch to process your inbox, and shrink to one minute when you need to get through a pile quickly. The number is not the point — small actions should never be allowed to pile up into a list.

One condition is usually dropped, and it matters: the rule only applies if the task needs doing at all. If it does not, delete it — doing a useless task quickly is still doing a useless task.

Why small tasks are so expensive

The first reason a deferred task costs more than two minutes is that your mind will not leave it alone. In 1927, the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik published a study showing that people remember unfinished tasks better than finished ones. Her participants were given small tasks, half of them interrupted before completion. Asked afterwards what they had done, they recalled the interrupted tasks about 90% better than the ones they had finished. An unfinished task stays active in memory, like a song left half-sung.

That is the Zeigarnik effect, and it explains why a pile of small jobs feels heavier than the sum of its parts. Each open task is a thread your mind keeps pulling at. Ten small tasks deferred in a day become fifty open loops by Friday — fifty small claims on your attention, none urgent enough to act on, all present enough to distract you.

Finishing a two-minute task closes the loop: the tension disappears the moment it is done, and the mind lets it go. That is the quiet reward of the rule — not just a shorter list, but a quieter head.

The switching tax

The second reason is the cost of switching. In a field study published at the CHI conference in 2005, Gloria Mark and her colleagues shadowed information workers at work. When a task was interrupted, it took an average of 25 minutes and 26 seconds before the worker returned to it — after typically working through about two other tasks first. About 77% of interrupted work was resumed the same day, but only after that long detour.

A follow-up experiment in 2008 found something surprising: interrupted workers actually finished faster than uninterrupted ones. The price was not speed but strain — significantly more stress, frustration, time pressure, and effort.

The American Psychological Association, summarising David Meyer’s research at the University of Michigan, put a number on the same problem: even brief mental blocks created by shifting between tasks can cost as much as 40% of someone’s productive time. A deferred two-minute task is therefore never just two minutes later. It is the doing, plus the reopening, the re-reading, the re-deciding, and the interruption of whatever you were doing when you finally picked it up again.

The maths of doing it now

Put the rule to work on an ordinary week: ten small tasks cross your desk each day — emails to answer, approvals to give, calls to return, forms to sign — each genuinely taking about two minutes.

One small taskDo it nowDefer it
Decide what it isonce, while holding itagain, when you reopen it
Do the work2 minutes2 minutes
Reopen and re-read it later0 minutesabout 2 minutes
Decide again0 minutesabout 1 minute
Mental costclosed — forgottenopen loop, nagging
Totalabout 2 minutesabout 5 minutes

Scale it to the week: done immediately, ten tasks a day cost 20 minutes a day, or 100 minutes a week; deferred, about 50 minutes a day, or 250 a week. The difference is 150 minutes — two and a half hours — every week.

Do it nowDefer it
Per day (10 tasks)20 minutesabout 50 minutes
Per week (5 days)100 minutesabout 250 minutes
Saved each week150 minutes — 2.5 hours
Saved each year (50 weeks)125 hours — about 15.6 working days

That is about three working weeks a year, recovered from tasks that each take two minutes — and the count is generous to deferring, assuming every deferred task is reopened only once, and never forgotten, misfiled, or chased by someone else. At the scale of a single afternoon, twenty small tasks take 40 minutes to clear: less than one meeting.

How to use the rule well

A good rule badly used becomes a bad habit, and the two-minute rule has one famous trap: stop for every two-minute task that appears, and you will spend the day doing nothing but two-minute tasks. The rule belongs to one moment — the moment you are processing. Use it while you clear your inbox or tray, not in the middle of deep work. When a quick task appears while you are concentrating, capture it on a list and handle it in your next processing round.

  1. Ask three questions. Can it be done in under two minutes? Does it need doing at all? Am I the one who should do it? If it is not yours, delegate it — which itself takes about two minutes.
  2. Process, then do. Run the rule when you open the inbox, not when you are writing the report. Separate the sorting from the working.
  3. Run a daily sweep. Ten minutes at the end of the day to clear the small items that arrived while you were busy. The desk is empty when you leave, and the morning starts clean.
  4. Batch what is left. Anything over two minutes goes on a list with a next action and a date. It is no longer a small task; it is a piece of work, and it deserves a slot.
  5. Keep the bar honest. If it takes three minutes and you are already holding it, do it anyway. The point is the pile, not the stopwatch.

The rule will not make you a different person. It will make your days feel different: fewer loose ends, fewer apologies for the small thing that slipped, fewer evenings spent remembering what you forgot. Two minutes is a small price; the pile is the expensive part.

What is sitting on your list right now that would take less than two minutes — and what would your week feel like if it were already done?

Key takeaways

  • David Allen’s two-minute rule (Getting Things Done, 2001): if the next action takes under two minutes, do it the moment it is defined.
  • Unfinished tasks stay in the mind: Zeigarnik (1927) found interrupted tasks were recalled about 90% better than completed ones.
  • Interrupted work takes an average of 25 minutes and 26 seconds to resume, after about two other tasks, and about 77% of it is resumed the same day (Mark et al., CHI 2005).
  • Switching between tasks can cost as much as 40% of productive time (American Psychological Association, 2006).
  • Ten small tasks a day, done now, cost 20 minutes; deferred, about 50 — a difference of 150 minutes a week, or 125 hours a year.
  • Use the rule while processing your inbox, not in the middle of deep work.

Sources

  • Allen D., Getting Things Done: The Art of Stress-Free Productivity, Penguin, 2001 (revised edition 2015) — the two-minute rule, see the Two-Minute Rule at gettingthingsdone.com
  • Zeigarnik B., “On Finished and Unfinished Tasks,” Psychologische Forschung, 1927;9:1–85 — see the abstract at APA PsycNet and the APA Dictionary of Psychology entry
  • Mark G., Gonzalez V. M., Harris J., “No Task Left Behind? Examining the Nature of Fragmented Work,” Proceedings of CHI 2005 — doi.org/10.1145/1054972.1055017
  • Mark G., Gudith D., Klocke U., “The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress,” Proceedings of CHI 2008 — doi.org/10.1145/1357054.1357072
  • American Psychological Association, “Multitasking: Switching Costs,” 20 March 2006 — apa.org

Note: the research figures come from the studies cited above. The time-saving example is arithmetic from the stated assumptions: ten small tasks a day, two minutes each to do now, about five each if deferred, five working days a week, fifty weeks a year.

articles.title: If Your Bank Failed, Is Your Money Safe?
articles.excerpt: Banks can fail — and they do. But in most of the world, your deposits are protected by law, up to a clear limit. Here is how the safety net works, what it covers, and how to make sure every dollar you hold is inside it.
articles.body_html:
Imagine waking up to a headline: your bank has failed. The doors are closed, the app will not open, and your savings — years of work — sit inside an institution that no longer exists. For most people, this is the nightmare that sits quietly behind every deposit they make.

It is a fair fear. Banks do fail. But here is the part almost nobody is told: in the United States, Europe, the United Kingdom, and most of the developed world, your deposits are protected by law — up to a clear, published limit. The safety net is real, it has worked for nearly a century, and it costs you nothing. You only need to know how it works.

Why banks can fail — and why that is normal

A bank does not keep your money in a vault. It lends most of it out — to homebuyers, businesses, and governments — and keeps only a fraction in reserve. This is how banking has worked for centuries, and it is how your savings earn interest. But it also means that if too many depositors ask for their money at once, even a healthy bank can run out of cash on hand. That is what a bank run is — and in the early 1930s, runs destroyed more than one-third of America's banks.

The answer was not to ban banking. It was to insure it. In 1933, the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation — the FDIC — and the idea spread around the world. The promise is simple: if your bank fails, the insurance pays you back, up to the limit.

Protected by law — deposit insurance means a bank's failure is a problem for its shareholders, not for its savers.

The $250,000 promise

In the United States, the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category. The coverage is automatic — you do not apply for it, and you do not pay for it; the banks pay the premiums. It is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government, and since the FDIC began in 1933, no depositor has ever lost a penny of insured funds — not in the Great Depression, not in 2008, not when three large banks failed in 2023.

Three words in that promise do most of the work:

  • Per bank — $250,000 at one bank and $250,000 at another are each fully covered. That is $500,000 of protection.
  • Per category — single accounts, joint accounts, and certain retirement accounts each get their own $250,000 limit at the same bank.
  • Per depositor — in a joint account, each co-owner is insured up to $250,000, so a $500,000 joint account held by two people is fully covered.

What is covered: checking accounts, savings accounts, money market deposit accounts, and certificates of deposit. What is not covered: stocks, bonds, mutual funds, cryptocurrency, and the contents of a safe deposit box — and insurance does not protect against theft or fraud. Those are different risks, with different protections.

The limit has grown with the times. When the FDIC began, it covered $2,500. Today it covers $250,000 — one hundred times more. The principle never changed: ordinary deposits are protected, so that a bank's failure is a problem for its shareholders, not for its savers.

The same idea, around the world

Almost every developed country runs the same system under a different name:

Country / regionSchemeLimit per depositor
United StatesFDIC$250,000
European UnionNational deposit guarantee schemes€100,000
United KingdomFSCS£120,000

The details differ — the British limit rose from £85,000 to £120,000 on 1 December 2025 — but the logic is identical everywhere: a published limit, a fund paid for by the banks, and a promise that ordinary savers come first.

One warning travels with the table: the limit usually applies per banking licence, not per brand. Two banks with different names can belong to the same group and share one licence — in that case, the limit covers your total across both. Always check the licence, not the logo.

A worked example: is $400,000 safe?

Meet Layla. She has $400,000 in a single savings account at one bank. If that bank failed tomorrow, the FDIC would pay her $250,000 — and $150,000 would be uninsured. She has not done anything wrong; she has simply kept too much in one place, under one ownership category.

Now watch what small changes do to the same $400,000:

ArrangementInsuredUninsured
$400,000 in one single account, one bank$250,000$150,000
$200,000 at Bank A + $200,000 at Bank B$400,000$0
$250,000 single account + $150,000 joint account, same bank$400,000$0

A couple can go further at a single bank: a $250,000 single account, a $500,000 joint account, and a $250,000 retirement account are three different ownership categories — each with its own limit, and the joint account covers $250,000 per co-owner. That is $1,000,000 of protection at one bank, entirely within the rules.

The lesson is not to move your money in fear. It is to count once, and arrange deliberately.

What to do this week

You do not need a perfect plan. You need four small steps:

  1. 1. Confirm your bank is insured. In the United States, check the FDIC's BankFind tool; in the United Kingdom, look for the FSCS Protected badge; in the European Union, ask your bank which national scheme covers it. If your bank is not covered, that is the first thing to fix.
  2. 2. Add up each ownership category at each bank. Single accounts together, joint accounts together, retirement accounts together. The limit applies to the total in each category, not to each account.
  3. 3. Spread anything above the limit. A second bank, or a different ownership category, turns uninsured money into insured money — with no change in how much you own.
  4. 4. Check the licence, not the brand. Two banks under one licence share one limit. And remember what insurance does not cover: investments, cryptocurrency, and fraud need their own protections.

The quiet confidence of a promise kept

Trust in banks is not built on marble columns or grand lobbies. It is built on a promise that has been kept, without exception, since 1933. A promise is only as good as its record — and this one has a record of more than ninety years, and zero insured depositors lost.

Your savings are the result of years of work. Knowing exactly how they are protected takes twenty minutes. Is your money inside the safety net — or sitting just outside it?

Key takeaways

  • Banks can fail — deposit insurance exists so that savers do not pay for it.
  • In the United States, the FDIC covers $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
  • Since 1933, no depositor has ever lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds.
  • The European Union protects €100,000 per depositor per bank; the United Kingdom's FSCS covers £120,000 since 1 December 2025.
  • $400,000 in one single account leaves $150,000 uninsured — split it, and all of it is covered.
  • The limit applies per banking licence, not per brand — check the licence.
  • Insurance covers deposits, not investments, cryptocurrency, or fraud.

Sources

  • Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) — Understanding Deposit Insurance: the $250,000 limit per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category; no insured depositor has lost funds since 1933.
  • Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) — Safeguarding the Nation's Savings: FDIC insurance backed by the full faith and credit of the United States government.
  • Bank of England / Prudential Regulation Authority — FSCS deposit protection limit increased to £120,000 from 1 December 2025 (previously £85,000 since 2017).
  • Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) — Deposit protection limit: £120,000 per eligible person, per authorised firm.
  • European Union, Directive 2014/49/EU — Deposit Guarantee Schemes Directive: harmonised protection of €100,000 per depositor, per bank.

Note: the $400,000 worked example and the $1,000,000 couple example are arithmetic worked from the FDIC's stated ownership-category rules. Limits change over time — always confirm the current figure with the scheme itself before making a decision.

articles.title: The Checklist Effect: How One Page of Boxes Saves Lives, Money, and Time
articles.excerpt: A single page of boxes cut surgical deaths nearly in half and wiped out two-thirds of intensive-care infections. The lesson is not about medicine — it is about how any team can make excellence routine.
articles.body_html:
On 30 October 1935, the most advanced bomber of its day crashed moments after takeoff. The Boeing Model 299 — the prototype of what would become the B-17 — stalled at 300 feet over Wright Field in Ohio and fell in flames. Two of the country’s finest test pilots died. The inquiry found nothing wrong with the aircraft. The pilot had simply forgotten to release a small lock that held the tail controls still while the aeroplane sat on the ground.

The machine had become too complex for even the best memory. The answer was not a better pilot. It was a piece of paper: a pilot’s checklist, read aloud before every takeoff. That single page saved the aeroplane, and it went on to become standard practice in every cockpit in the world.

Ninety years later, the same piece of paper is still saving lives — in operating rooms, in intensive care units, and in ordinary offices. The checklist is the cheapest management tool ever invented, and the most underused. This article shows what the evidence says, and how to use it.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

The operating room proves it

In 2008, the World Health Organization introduced a 19-item Surgical Safety Checklist, designed to improve team communication and consistency of care. It was tested in eight hospitals in eight cities — from Toronto and London to New Delhi, Manila, Amman, Auckland, Seattle, and Ifakara in Tanzania — between October 2007 and September 2008. Researchers followed 3,733 patients before the checklist and 3,955 after it. The results, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2009, were startling.

Outcome within 30 daysBefore the checklistAfter the checklistChange
Deaths1.5%0.8%a fall of 47%
Major complications11.0%7.0%a fall of 36%

The checklist took only a few minutes, at three pause points: before anaesthesia, before the first incision, and before the patient left the room. At each pause, the team stopped, confirmed the essentials out loud, and only then continued. The effect appeared in every hospital in the study, rich and poor alike.

Put the numbers in human terms. Applied to the study’s two groups, the old death rate implies about 56 deaths among the first 3,733 patients, and the new rate about 32 among the next 3,955. A page of boxes, read aloud, stood between those two numbers.

The intensive care unit proves it again

Three years earlier, in Michigan, a similar experiment was under way. Intensive care doctors knew that infections from central lines — tubes placed in large veins — were killing patients, and they knew how to prevent them. Yet the infections kept happening. Dr Peter Pronovost of Johns Hopkins reduced the prevention guidance to a checklist of five steps: wash hands, clean the skin with antiseptic, use full sterile barriers, avoid the groin site where possible, and remove the line as soon as it is no longer needed.

The checklist was rolled out across 103 intensive care units in Michigan. Within three months, the median infection rate fell from 2.7 infections per 1,000 catheter-days to zero. The reduction — up to 66% — was sustained across the 18 months of the study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2006, and an estimated 1,500 lives were saved in the first 18 months.

Notice what the checklist did not do. It taught nobody anything new. Every doctor already knew all five steps. The problem was never knowledge. It was the gap between knowing and doing, every single time, under pressure, at three in the morning. The checklist closed that gap.

Why a piece of paper beats a brilliant memory

Atul Gawande, the surgeon who led the WHO checklist study, wrote a book about it: The Checklist Manifesto (2009). His argument is simple. In every field, the volume of knowledge has outgrown any single mind. A surgeon, a pilot, or a manager can be excellent and still fail, because excellence now depends on dozens of small steps, done in the right order, by several people, under time pressure. Memory is the weakest link in that chain.

A good checklist works for three reasons. First, it catches the step that memory drops when attention is stretched — the gust lock, the antibiotic, the attachment. Second, it creates a pause: a moment when the whole team stops, looks at each other, and confirms the plan out loud. That pause is where communication happens. Third, it turns one person’s expertise into a routine the whole team can follow, so quality no longer depends on who happens to be on duty.

This is why the checklist is an administration tool before it is a medical one. It is a system for making good practice repeatable. And repeatable good practice is the whole job of administration.

The arithmetic of a checklist at the office

Now take the same idea out of the hospital and into an ordinary office. Take a team of six people. Each of them loses about 90 minutes a week to rework caused by missed steps: the attachment that was never sent, the approval that was never requested, the handover missing one crucial detail. That is nine hours a week across the team, and 468 hours a year. Suppose a simple ten-item checklist — checked before a report goes out, before a handover, before a client file is closed — cuts that rework in half.

Without a checklistWith a checklist
Rework per week9.0 hours4.5 hours
Rework per year468 hours234 hours
Value of lost time at $30 an hour$14,040 a year$7,020 a year

The checklist recovers 234 hours a year — about 29 working days — and about $7,020 of value, for a page that costs nothing to write. The numbers are an illustration, but the shape of them is the point: small errors, repeated daily, are expensive; small corrections, repeated daily, are valuable.

How to build a checklist that actually gets used

Most checklists fail for the same reason most resolutions fail: they are too long, too vague, or never tested. Five rules keep one alive.

  1. Keep it short. Five to nine items, on one page. If it needs a second page, it is a manual, not a checklist.
  2. Put pause points where mistakes are expensive. Before sending, before signing, before a handover — the moments when an error becomes hard to undo.
  3. Give every action one owner and one deadline. A step with no name on it belongs to nobody.
  4. Test it on a real task within a week. A checklist nobody has tried is a wish, not a tool.
  5. Review it monthly. Remove steps that never fail, and add the step that just failed. A checklist that never changes is a checklist nobody reads.

The checklist does not make you less skilled. It makes your skill reliable. The best pilot in 1935 died because of a step his memory dropped; the pilots who followed him flew safely for decades, not because they were better, but because they had a page. Your work deserves the same protection.

What is the one repeated task in your week that fails most often — and what would its five-item checklist say?

Key takeaways

  • A forgotten gust lock crashed the Model 299 in 1935 — and gave aviation the preflight checklist.
  • The WHO 19-item surgical checklist cut deaths from 1.5% to 0.8% and complications from 11.0% to 7.0% (New England Journal of Medicine, 2009).
  • In 103 Michigan intensive care units, a five-step checklist cut central-line infections by up to 66%, with the median rate falling to zero (New England Journal of Medicine, 2006).
  • Checklists work because they catch skipped steps, force a pause, and turn expertise into routine.
  • A team of six losing 90 minutes each a week to rework can recover 234 hours a year — about 29 working days — with a checklist that halves the errors.
  • A good checklist has 5–9 items, fits on one page, and is reviewed every month.

Sources

  • Haynes AB, Weiser TG, Berry WR, et al., “A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population,” New England Journal of Medicine, 2009;360:491–499 — see the full text at PubMed Central and the World Health Organization summary
  • Pronovost P, Needham D, Berenholtz S, et al., “An Intervention to Decrease Catheter-Related Bloodstream Infections in the ICU,” New England Journal of Medicine, 2006;355:2725–2732 — see the abstract at Medscape
  • Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum, “On. Set. Checked.” — how the 1935 Model 299 crash gave aviation the checklist
  • Gawande A., The Checklist Manifesto: How to Get Things Right, Metropolitan Books, 2009

Note: the medical figures come from the peer-reviewed studies cited above. The office example is arithmetic from the stated assumptions — a team of six, 90 minutes of rework a week each, a 50% reduction from the checklist, $30 an hour.

articles.title: Ten Years of Waiting Costs $281,000
articles.excerpt: Two people save the same $200 a month. One starts at 25, the other at 35 — and at 65 the first has about $525,000 while the second has about $244,000. The difference is $281,000, and the late starter contributed only $24,000 less. Time, not money, is the ingredient that cannot be bought back.
articles.body_html:
Two people earn the same salary. They live in similar homes, drive similar cars, and both decide to set aside the same $200 a month. The only difference between them is the calendar. One starts at twenty-five. The other waits until thirty-five. At sixty-five, the first has about $525,000. The second has about $244,000. The difference is $281,000 — and the one who waited contributed only $24,000 less.

That is the price of ten years. Not ten years of spending, or ten years of bad luck, but ten years of waiting for a better moment to begin. The money was never the problem. Time was.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

The arithmetic of waiting

Take $200 a month, invested steadily, earning an average of 7% a year after inflation — the long-run real return of the broad stock market, explained below. Nothing clever, nothing risky, no lucky stock pick. Just the same deposit, every month, left alone to grow. The result depends almost entirely on when the first deposit is made.

Start ageYears investedTotal contributedValue at 65
2540$96,000about $525,000
3035$84,000about $360,000
3530$72,000about $244,000
4025$60,000about $162,000
4520$48,000about $104,000

Read the table from the bottom up and the pattern is unmistakable: every decade of waiting removes far more from the ending than it saves in contributions. The person who starts at forty-five contributes half as much as the one who starts at twenty-five, yet ends with one-fifth of the money. The missing $421,000 was never contributed by anyone. It is the growth that the missing years would have produced.

Most people are on the wrong side of this table. The Federal Reserve’s 2025 household survey found that only 35% of adults who had not yet retired thought their retirement saving was on track — even though 61% held a retirement account of some kind. The accounts exist. The plan, for most people, does not.

Why the first decade is worth eleven times its weight

The $281,000 gap is not mysterious once you look at where it comes from. The early starter’s only advantage is the $24,000 contributed during the first ten years — $200 a month from twenty-five to thirty-five. But that $24,000 then has thirty to forty years to grow, and growth on growth is where the money is made. Of the early starter’s $525,000, only $96,000 was ever contributed; $429,000 is growth. Of the late starter’s $244,000, $172,000 is growth. The extra $24,000 of contributions produced about $281,000 of extra ending value — every dollar contributed in that first decade is worth about $11.70 at sixty-five.

That is why delay is so expensive even in small doses. Waiting one year at twenty-five — starting at twenty-six instead — costs about $38,000 by sixty-five. Waiting five years costs about $165,000. The years that feel cheapest to waste, when retirement is a distant rumour, are precisely the years that matter most, because they are the years with the longest runway ahead of them.

And this is not an artefact of choosing a generous return. At 5% a year, the ten-year gap is still about $139,000. At 8%, it is about $400,000. Whatever the market delivers, the cost of waiting stays enormous — because the cost comes from time, not from the rate.

The 7% assumption, stated honestly

A careful reader should ask where 7% comes from. The broad U.S. stock market, measured by the S&P 500 index with dividends reinvested, has averaged about 10% a year since 1928, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices data. After adjusting for inflation of roughly 3% a year, the real return — the growth in actual purchasing power — is about 7%. That is why 7% is the standard planning figure: it is the market’s long-run average, stated in today’s money.

But an average is not a promise. The market has fallen by a third in a single year and stayed flat for a decade. Somebody who starts in a bad decade will earn less than 7%; somebody who starts in a good one will earn more. The honest statement is this: nobody can know the return of the next forty years, but every decade of history says that starting early beats starting late at almost any return. The tables above assume the money stays invested through the falls as well as the rises — selling in a panic is the one decision that breaks the arithmetic entirely.

“I am already late” — start anyway

The most dangerous reading of this article is the one that ends in resignation: I am thirty-five, or forty-five, and the best years are gone, so what is the point? The point is in the same table. Starting at forty-five, $200 a month still turns $48,000 of contributions into about $104,000 — more than double what was put in. Starting at thirty-five with $300 a month ends at about $366,000, comfortably ahead of the twenty-five-year-old who saved only $100 a month and ended at about $262,000. A larger amount can compensate for a later start; nothing compensates for never starting.

Nor does the amount need to be large. Two hundred dollars a month is about $6.58 a day — less than many people spend without noticing. The question is never whether the amount is impressive. It is whether it is automatic, and whether it begins this month rather than next year.

  1. 1. Start with any amount you can sustain — $50 or $100 a month counts; the habit matters more than the size.
  2. 2. Automate it for payday, so the money is invested before it can be spent.
  3. 3. Raise the amount with every pay rise, before the new income becomes the new normal.
  4. 4. Stay invested through market falls; the falls are when the monthly deposits buy the most.
  5. 5. Review once a year, and never measure progress against someone who started ten years earlier — measure it against not starting at all.

Time is the only ingredient you cannot buy back

Money can be earned later. Knowledge can be learned later. But the years a deposit spends growing cannot be purchased at any price — the market does not sell them. The person who starts at twenty-five did not work harder, earn more, or know some secret. They simply began while beginning was cheap, and let the calendar do the heavy work.

The best day to start was ten years ago. The second-best day is today. What will your money be doing while you wait?

Key takeaways

  • $200 a month at 7% a year grows to about $525,000 if started at 25, but only about $244,000 if started at 35 — a $281,000 gap for just $24,000 more contributed.
  • Every dollar contributed in the first decade is worth about $11.70 at 65; waiting one year at 25 costs about $38,000, and five years costs about $165,000.
  • The cost of waiting holds at any reasonable return: at 5% the ten-year gap is still about $139,000; at 8% it is about $400,000.
  • The S&P 500 has averaged about 10% a year since 1928, or about 7% after inflation (S&P Dow Jones Indices) — an average, not a guarantee.
  • Only 35% of non-retired adults think their retirement saving is on track (Federal Reserve, 2025 survey), even though 61% hold a retirement account.
  • Starting late still works: $200 a month from 45 becomes about $104,000, and $300 a month from 35 becomes about $366,000.
  • Automate the deposit on payday, raise it with every pay rise, and stay invested through market falls.

Sources

  • S&P Dow Jones Indices, S&P 500 total return data — the index has averaged about 10% a year since 1928 with dividends reinvested, or about 7% after inflation; see The Motley Fool, “What Is the Average Stock Market Return?” and J.P. Morgan Chase, “What Is the Average Stock Market Return?”
  • Federal Reserve, “Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025”, May 2026 — only 35% of non-retired adults thought their retirement saving was on track; 61% held a tax-preferred retirement account.

Note: all tables are arithmetic from the stated assumptions — $200 a month, 7% a year compounded monthly, held to age 65. Returns are illustrative averages, not a promise of future results; investing involves risk, including loss of principal.

articles.title: Your Emergency Fund Needs Its Own Home
articles.excerpt: Emergencies do not send a warning — and most people are one surprise bill away from borrowing. The Federal Reserve found that only 63% of adults could cover a $400 expense with cash; the fund that protects you is built in a separate account, one small automatic transfer at a time.
articles.body_html:
Picture a Tuesday like any other. The car will not start. The water heater is leaking. Or the phone call comes, and the job is gone, and the next paycheque is not coming. Nothing about the day was unusual until it was. The question is never whether a day like that arrives. It arrives for everyone, sooner or later. The question is whether there is money standing between that day and the rest of your life.

That money has a name: an emergency fund. It is not savings for a holiday, a new phone, or a better car. It is the money that turns a bad week into a bad week — instead of a bad year. And it works best when it lives in its own home, separate from everything else you own.

All figures in this article come from the sources cited at the end.

How much is enough?

The standard guidance is three to six months of essential expenses — not three to six months of income, but of the money you must spend to keep living: rent, food, bills, transport, medicine. Three months covers most surprises; six months covers the long ones, like a job lost in a slow market. The number sounds large until you price it against the alternative: borrowing at the worst possible moment.

If three to six months feels impossible, start smaller. The first milestone is $1,000 — enough to absorb the everyday emergencies: a car repair, a broken appliance, a dental bill. Most emergencies are small; it is the small ones, unhandled, that become debts.

The surveys say most people are not there yet. Bankrate’s 2025 Emergency Savings Report found that only 41% of Americans would pay a $1,000 emergency expense from savings — the other 59% would have to borrow, cut back, or find the money another way. The Federal Reserve’s 2025 household survey found that 63% of adults would cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent, and that only 55% had set aside three months of expenses. In the same survey, 59% said they had faced at least one major unexpected expense in the previous twelve months. Emergencies are not rare. Being unready for them is the common condition.

Monthly essential expensesStarter fundThree monthsSix months
$1,000$1,000$3,000$6,000
$1,500$1,000$4,500$9,000
$2,000$1,000$6,000$12,000
$3,000$1,000$9,000$18,000

Read the table the other way round, and it stops looking frightening: the starter fund is the same $1,000 for everyone, whatever the household spends. The full fund is a destination you walk toward, not a wall you must climb in a day.

Why it needs its own home

The amount matters less than the address. An emergency fund kept in the same account as everyday money is not an emergency fund; it is a balance that happens to be high today. The rent, the groceries, the small pleasures — all of them draw from the same pool, and the fund is spent a little at a time, without any single decision ever feeling like a raid on it.

The psychologist Richard Thaler gave this a name: mental accounting. People treat money differently depending on where it sits and what it is labelled, even though a dollar is a dollar. A separate account turns that quirk into a tool: money labelled for emergencies only, sitting in its own place, is money the mind leaves alone. Distance is the best protection.

Separation also changes what happens on the bad day itself. When the emergency arrives, there is no agonising over whether the money can be spared from the holiday budget or the rent — the answer is already written on the account. And when the fund is used, the hole it leaves is visible, which is exactly what makes rebuilding it a priority instead of a vague intention.

Where to keep it

The fund has three jobs, and they narrow the choice quickly. It must be reachable within a day or two. It must be safe — its value must not fall the week you need it. And it should earn something, because money standing still quietly loses value. A savings account meets all three; the stock market fails the second, since an emergency does not wait for a market recovery.

Not all savings accounts pay the same. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation puts the national average savings rate at 0.38% a year, as of October 2026. High-yield savings accounts — the same kind of account, usually online, with the same federal insurance of up to $250,000 per depositor per bank — pay around 4%. On $10,000, the difference is $38 a year against $400.

Where $10,000 sits for one yearRateInterest earned
Average savings account0.38%$38
High-yield savings accountabout 4%about $400

The rate is not the point of the fund — the fund exists to be there, not to grow rich — but $362 a year is a free upgrade for moving the money to a different shelf in the same safe. Rates change with the market, so check the current rate before choosing; the principle does not change: the fund should work while it waits.

How to build it

The method is unglamorous, and that is why it works. Automate a transfer for the day your income arrives, before the money can be spent on anything else. A small amount, sent automatically, beats a large amount that depends on willpower at the end of the month — because at the end of the month, the money is usually gone.

Automatic transferTime to reach $1,000Total in one year
$25 a week40 weeks$1,300
$50 a week20 weeks$2,600
$100 a month10 months$1,200
$200 a month5 months$2,400

The order matters too. First, the $1,000 starter fund. Then, if there is high-interest debt, attack it — a fund earning 4% while a card charges 20% is a leak, not a plan. Then build toward the full three to six months. And when a windfall arrives — a tax refund, a bonus, a sold item — send part of it straight to the fund before it can become spending money.

  1. 1. Open a separate savings account — ideally a high-yield one — and name it for its purpose.
  2. 2. Set an automatic transfer for payday, even $25 a week.
  3. 3. Keep the starter goal in sight: $1,000 first, then three months of expenses.
  4. 4. Use the fund only for true emergencies — the broken car, the lost job, the hospital bill — and rebuild it immediately after.
  5. 5. Review the target once a year, as expenses change, and raise the transfer when income rises.

The fund that buys you calm

The return on an emergency fund is not the interest. It is the sleep. The person with three months of expenses set aside faces the same broken car as everyone else — but the repair is an errand, not a crisis, and a lost job is a setback to manage, not a cliff to fall from. The fund does not prevent bad days. It decides how long they last.

Start tonight: open the separate account, set the first transfer, and give your future self a home for the money that protects everything else. What would change in your life if the next surprise were already paid for?

Key takeaways

  • An emergency fund is three to six months of essential expenses, kept separate from everyday money; the first milestone is $1,000.
  • Only 41% of Americans would pay a $1,000 emergency from savings (Bankrate, 2025); 59% would have to borrow or find the money another way.
  • The Federal Reserve found that 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or its equivalent, and 55% had three months of expenses saved (2025 survey).
  • Money in a separate account is money the mind leaves alone — mental accounting (Thaler, 1999) turns distance into protection.
  • The national average savings rate is 0.38% a year (FDIC, October 2026); high-yield accounts pay around 4% — $38 against $400 on $10,000.
  • $25 a week reaches the $1,000 starter in 40 weeks; $50 a week in 20 weeks. Automate the transfer on payday.
  • Order: starter fund first, then high-interest debt, then the full three to six months.

Sources

  • Federal Reserve, “Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households in 2025”, May 2026 — 63% of adults would cover a $400 emergency expense with cash or its equivalent; 55% had set aside three months of expenses; 59% had faced at least one major unexpected expense in the previous twelve months.
  • Bankrate, “2025 Emergency Savings Report” — only 41% of Americans would pay a $1,000 emergency expense from savings; survey of U.S. adults, 6–9 December 2024; published 23 January 2025.
  • Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, “National Rates and Rate Caps,” October 2026 — national average savings rate 0.38% a year as of 19 October 2026; deposits insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank.
  • Richard H. Thaler, “Mental Accounting Matters,” Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 1999, 12(3), 183–206 — people treat money differently depending on the account it sits in and the label it carries.

Note: the 4% high-yield figure is an illustration of rates available from online banks in late 2026; rates are variable and change with the market. All tables are arithmetic from the stated assumptions.
