articles.title: The Best Performer Is Not Always the Best Manager
articles.excerpt: The best salesperson gets promoted to lead the team — and within a year, sales fall, two people quit, and the star is miserable. Gallup’s research explains why: managing people is a different job, and only about one person in ten has the talent for it.
articles.body_html:
Every workplace knows this story. The best salesperson on the team is promoted to lead the team. Within a year, sales have fallen, two good people have quit, and the star performer is miserable. The promotion was meant as a reward. It behaved like a punishment — for everyone involved.

The promotion rewarded one skill and demanded another. Doing a job well and leading the people who do that job are two different jobs — not a bigger version of the first, but a different craft.

All figures in this article come from the Gallup research and the book cited in the Sources section.

Two different jobs

In 1969, the educator Laurence J. Peter gave this pattern a name: the Peter Principle. In a hierarchy, he wrote, people tend to rise to their level of incompetence — they keep being promoted for doing well until they reach a job they cannot do well, and there they stay.

Consider what changes on promotion day. Yesterday, success meant your own output; today, it means your team’s output: whether they hit their numbers, stay, and grow. The work that made you excellent is now the work you must stop doing — for work you have never practised.

Gallup asked managers why they believed they had been hired. The most common answers were success in a previous role, or tenure — neither says anything about whether the person can manage. Being a successful programmer, salesperson, or engineer is no guarantee of being adept at managing others.

What the numbers say

Gallup has studied managerial talent for five decades. Its conclusion is blunt: naming a manager is one of the most important decisions a company makes, and companies usually get it wrong.

FindingNumberSource
People who possess high talent to manageAbout 1 in 10Gallup, State of the American Manager
Management hiring decisions that miss the mark on talent82%Gallup, State of the American Manager
Share of the difference in team engagement that comes down to the managerAt least 70%Gallup, 11,781 work teams analysed
Current managers with high talent for managing18%Gallup
Current managers with basic talent for managing20%Gallup
Extra profit from managers with high or basic talent, vs. average managersAbout 48% higherGallup
U.S. employees who are engaged at work30%Gallup, State of the American Workplace
Employees worldwide who are engaged at work13%Gallup

The picture is stark. Only about one person in ten has the natural talent to manage at a high level — yet companies choose the wrong person for the job 82% of the time. The two numbers explain each other: if the talent is rare and the selection ignores it, most managers will not have it. And the cost lands on everyone, because the manager accounts for at least 70% of the difference in how engaged a team is.

There is good news too: another two people in ten have some of the basic talent and can function at a high level with coaching, so the pool is closer to three in ten — and they are worth finding, contributing about 48% higher profit than average managers between them.

The cost of one wrong promotion

A wrong promotion is expensive in two directions: the team loses a manager it never had, and the star performer it used to have. Put numbers on a small team and the bill becomes concrete.

Take a team of eight people, each earning an average of $50,000 a year — a payroll of $400,000. The best performer is promoted to manage them. Within a year, two of the eight quit. Gallup puts the cost of replacing one employee at one-half to two times their annual salary, and calls that a conservative estimate.

What one wrong promotion costsNumber
Team size8 people
Average salary$50,000
Team payroll$400,000 a year
People who quit within a year2
Cost to replace one person (one-half to two times salary)$25,000–$100,000
Cost to replace both$50,000–$200,000
Replacement cost as a share of the team’s payroll12.5%–50%

That is the visible bill: $50,000 to $200,000 to replace two people, on a $400,000 payroll. And that is only the visible bill: the promoted star no longer does the work they were best at, so the team’s best output is gone too. Gallup found that 52% of people who quit voluntarily said their manager or organisation could have prevented them leaving, and 51% said nobody had spoken to them about their satisfaction or future in the three months before they left. Most exits are a conversation that never happened.

Scale the same arithmetic up, and the numbers become national. Gallup estimates voluntary turnover costs U.S. businesses about $1 trillion a year, and active disengagement $450 billion to $550 billion a year in lost productivity. A hundred-person organisation paying an average salary of $50,000, with the 26.3% turnover rate in Gallup’s example, faces replacement costs of roughly $660,000 to $2.6 million a year.

What to do instead

The answer is not to stop promoting good people. It is to promote them for the right reasons.

1. Promote on talent, not on track record alone. Past performance is evidence about the old job. Look for the talents Gallup finds in great managers: motivating people, assertiveness, a culture of accountability, relationships built on trust, and decisions made on productivity rather than politics.

2. Build a second ladder. If the only way to earn more is to manage people, your best performers will demand jobs they do not want and cannot do. Create a senior expert track — with pay, title, and standing equal to management — so a brilliant specialist is not forced into a job that wastes them.

3. Coach the two in ten. Another two people in ten can manage at a high level if the company invests in coaching and development. That is the largest untapped pool of managers in any organisation — and cheaper than replacing the people a bad manager drives away.

4. Try the role before the title — and ask the team. Let a candidate lead a project or run the team for a month while their old role is still theirs to return to. A trial tells both sides the truth cheaply. And look at who the team already turns to for help: with about one manager for every ten employees and one person in ten holding the talent, someone on each team probably has it — usually not the current manager.

The best performer is not always the best manager — and that is not a flaw in the performer, but a fact about two different jobs. Promote the performer into a bigger version of what they already do brilliantly, and the manager into the job of making others brilliant. Get it right, and the team keeps its star and gains a leader; get it wrong, and it loses both. Think of the best manager you ever had: was that person the best at the job before they managed — or the best at bringing out the best in others?

Key takeaways

  • Doing a job well and managing the people who do it are two different jobs — the Peter Principle is what happens when a promotion ignores that (Peter & Hull, 1969).
  • About one person in ten has high talent to manage, yet companies choose the wrong person 82% of the time (Gallup).
  • Managers account for at least 70% of the difference in team engagement — the largest single influence on how a team performs.
  • A wrong promotion costs twice: the team loses its star performer and gains a manager it did not need. Two departures from an eight-person team on $50,000 salaries cost $50,000–$200,000 to replace.
  • Another two in ten people can manage at a high level with coaching — the largest untapped pool of managers in any organisation.
  • Managers with high or basic talent contribute about 48% higher profit than average managers; companies that double engagement see about 147% higher earnings per share.
  • 52% of people who quit voluntarily said the departure could have been prevented — most exits are a conversation that never happened.

Sources

  • Jim Harter, “Why Great Managers Are So Rare,” Gallup, 2014, updated 16 February 2026 — 1 in 10 with high management talent; 82% of hiring decisions miss; managers account for at least 70% of engagement variance; 18% high talent and 20% basic talent among current managers, contributing about 48% higher profit; 30% of U.S. employees and 13% worldwide engaged; 147% higher earnings per share where engagement doubles.
  • Shane McFeely and Ben Wigert, “This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion,” Gallup, 13 March 2019 — replacing an employee costs one-half to two times annual salary; 100-person organisation at $50,000 average salary faces about $660,000 to $2.6 million a year; 52% of voluntary leavers said the departure could have been prevented; 51% had no conversation about satisfaction or future in their last three months.
  • Gallup, “State of the American Workplace,” 2013 — actively disengaged employees cost the U.S. $450 billion to $550 billion a year in lost productivity; 30% of U.S. workers engaged, 52% not engaged, 18% actively disengaged.
  • Laurence J. Peter and Raymond Hull, The Peter Principle: Why Things Always Go Wrong, William Morrow, 1969 — people in a hierarchy tend to rise to their level of incompetence.

Note: the team-of-eight example and its $50,000–$200,000 replacement range are arithmetic from Gallup’s one-half to two times salary range; Gallup’s own 100-person example ($660,000 to $2.6 million) is quoted from its 2019 article.

articles.title: Three Good Things Can Change Your Week
articles.excerpt: One bad moment can outweigh a whole day of good ones — unless you write the good ones down. A one-week exercise, tested in a published study, shows how three small lines a night can retrain what your mind notices.
articles.body_html:
Ask someone how their day went, and the answer usually starts with the one thing that went wrong. The nine things that went right barely get a mention — not because they did not happen, but because the mind files them differently. Bad moments are written in ink. Good moments are written in pencil, and the pencil fades by bedtime.

This is not a character flaw; it is how attention works. The encouraging part is that attention can be trained — in about five minutes a night. The exercise is called three good things: each night, for one week, write down three things that went well, and why each one went well. A published study found the effects were still measurable six months later.

All figures in this article come from the peer-reviewed studies cited in the Sources section.

Why the bad outweighs the good

In 2001, Roy Baumeister and his colleagues reviewed decades of psychology research under a blunt title: “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Across everyday events, relationships, learning and memory, the pattern was the same: bad events, bad feedback and bad information carry more psychological weight than good ones of the same size. A single criticism can outweigh a day of praise.

There is a reason for this, and it is not pessimism. For most of human history, missing a threat was far more costly than missing a reward, so the mind became a smoke alarm: quick to sound, slow to switch off. That alarm still runs today, where the “threats” are a sharp email or a missed deadline.

The result is a ledger that never balances: a day with nine good moments and one bad one gets filed under the bad one. The good moments are not forgotten because they were unimportant. They are forgotten because nobody wrote them down.

The experiment that asked for one week

In 2005, Martin Seligman and three colleagues tested five short happiness exercises against a placebo. Adults who signed up online were randomly assigned one exercise for a week, then followed up at one week, one month, three months and six months. The placebo group wrote about early memories each night. The three good things group wrote down, each night, three things that went well that day — and why each one went well.

The placebo gave a brief lift that faded within about a week. The three good things group looked different: happiness rose, depressive symptoms fell, and both changes were still visible six months later. Of the five exercises, it was one of only two with effects that lasted — and the people who benefited most kept the exercise going on their own after the week ended.

What the numbers actually say

Three good things was not the only gratitude exercise ever tested. Two years earlier, Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough ran three experiments on counting blessings, published in 2003. The pattern was consistent — and modest, which is exactly why it is believable.

StudyWhat people didWhat changed
Study 1 — 10 weeks, about 200 studentsListed up to five blessings each weekExercised 4.35 hours a week, against 3.01 in the hassles group; fewer physical symptoms; more optimistic about the week ahead
Study 2 — 13 days, daily listsListed blessings every dayHigher positive affect than the hassles group
Study 3 — 21 days, 65 adults with neuromuscular diseaseListed blessings every daySlept 7.58 hours a night, against 7.06 in the control group; more positive affect; felt more connected to others

The gratitude group exercised about an hour and a half more per week — 4.35 hours against 3.01 — and slept about half an hour more a night. These are real differences, not transformations. A 2012 replication found the same honest shape: happiness rose lastingly, but against a positive placebo, depressive symptoms did no better. A 2013 meta-analysis agreed — modest improvements. Modest is not nothing: a small effect, repeated every night, is how a habit earns its keep.

Why three, and why write it down

Three is a deliberate number. One is too easy — the mind picks the obvious one and stops. Ten is a chore, and a chore gets abandoned. Three is small enough to do every night and large enough to force a search: by the third item, you are noticing things you would otherwise have walked past — the colleague who helped without being asked.

The “why” matters as much as the “what”: explaining why a good thing happened trains the mind to see its own part in it. “My friend called because I have kept in touch for years” says the good thing is connected to something you did — and over a week, those explanations rewrite the story the mind tells.

And writing beats thinking: a thought at midnight can be edited, doubted and forgotten by morning, while a written list is evidence. When the bad day comes — and it will — the list is still there, saying the week was not only the bad day.

How to do it tonight

The exercise needs nothing but a notebook and five minutes. Do it at the same time each night, before bed, while the day is still fresh.

1. Write down three things that went well today. Be specific: “my colleague helped me finish the report” counts; “work was fine” does not.

2. Next to each one, write one line about why it went well. What caused it — and what part did you play?

3. Keep it to five minutes. If it takes longer, you are writing an essay, not a habit.

4. Do it for seven nights. Then decide whether to keep going — the largest gains belonged to the people who continued.

What one week costsNumber
Nights7
Minutes a night5
Minutes for the whole week35
Good things noticed21

And if the week becomes a habit, the arithmetic quietly grows: three things a night is 1,095 good things noticed in a year, for about 30 hours of writing — less time than a single working week. That is the whole price of retraining what your mind notices.

Tonight, before you sleep, try it: what three things went well today — and why? The answer will be waiting in the morning, when the bad moment tries to tell you the day was only ever the bad moment.

Key takeaways

  • Bad events carry more weight than good ones of the same size (Baumeister et al., 2001) — so good moments need writing down, or they fade.
  • In Seligman et al. (2005), one week of three good things raised happiness and lowered depressive symptoms, still measurable six months later.
  • The people who benefited most were the ones who kept the exercise going after the week ended.
  • In Emmons & McCullough (2003), the gratitude group exercised 4.35 hours a week against 3.01, and slept about half an hour more.
  • A 2012 replication and a 2013 meta-analysis agree: the effects are real and modest — not a treatment, but a habit worth keeping.
  • Three things a night, five minutes, seven nights: 21 good things noticed for 35 minutes of writing.

Sources

  • Martin E. P. Seligman, Tracy A. Steen, Nansook Park, and Christopher Peterson, “Positive Psychology Progress: Empirical Validation of Interventions,” American Psychologist, 2005, 60(5), 410–421 — effects still measurable at six months.
  • Robert A. Emmons and Michael E. McCullough, “Counting Blessings Versus Burdens,” Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2003, 84(2), 377–389 — exercise and sleep differences across three studies.
  • Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer, and Kathleen D. Vohs, “Bad Is Stronger Than Good,” Review of General Psychology, 2001, 5(4), 323–370.
  • Myriam Mongrain and Tracy Anselmo-Matthews, “Do Positive Psychology Exercises Work? A Replication of Seligman et al. (2005),” Journal of Clinical Psychology, 2012, 68(4), 382–389 — happiness gains replicated; no advantage over a positive placebo on depressive symptoms.
  • Linda Bolier, Merel Haverman, Gerben J. Westerhof, Heleen Riper, Filip Smit, and Ernst Bohlmeijer, “Positive Psychology Interventions: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Studies,” BMC Public Health, 2013, 13, 119 — modest improvements in well-being overall.

Note: the exercise and sleep hours are the published group averages from Emmons and McCullough (2003); the 21 good things and 35 minutes are arithmetic from the exercise itself.

articles.title: The Real Cost of a Meeting
articles.excerpt: One weekly hour with eight people costs $12,480 a year — and that is only the visible part. Meetings have a price tag, a hidden cost, and a habit of multiplying.
articles.body_html:
Walk into any office on any weekday and you will find the most expensive item on the agenda is the one nobody priced. A meeting is the only purchase an organisation makes every day without ever seeing the bill. The room is free, the coffee is free, and so everyone assumes the meeting is free. It is not. It is paid for in the only currency that cannot be refunded: the working hours of the people sitting in it.

Once you price a meeting honestly, two things happen. First, you stop being surprised that the week disappears. Second, you start treating the calendar the way a careful administrator treats a budget — as money, because that is what it is.

All dollar figures in this article are illustrative, worked from the stated assumptions.

The maths nobody does

Take an ordinary weekly meeting: eight people, one hour, an average cost of $30 an hour per person. The arithmetic is simple, and almost nobody does it.

Eight people at $30 an hour is $240 for that single hour. Held every week, that is $12,480 a year — for one meeting. And that is the small one. Put three ordinary recurring meetings side by side, and the total stops looking ordinary:

MeetingPeopleHourly costLengthCost per meetingCost per year
Team check-in5$2530 min$62.50$3,250
Department update8$3060 min$240$12,480
Leadership review10$4590 min$675$35,100
Total———$977.50$50,830

Three meetings. None of them large, none of them unusual. Together they cost $50,830 a year — roughly the salary of another full-time colleague — and they buy, in most weeks, a status update that could have been a written note. And $30 an hour is a conservative figure: a person earning $60,000 a year costs about $28.85 an hour in salary alone, and roughly $37.50 once benefits and overhead are counted. At senior levels, the numbers climb steeply.

The costs that never appear on the invoice

The salary maths is only the visible part of the bill. A meeting also charges a second price, in attention, and attention is the scarcest resource in any working day. Research by Gloria Mark at the University of California, Irvine found that after an interruption, it takes an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to get back to the work you were doing — and people usually handle about two other tasks in between. A meeting is an interruption with an invitation attached. Three interruptions a day cost roughly 70 minutes of refocusing — nearly six hours a week, spent getting back to where you already were.

Then there is the meeting after the meeting: the corridor conversation where the real decision is made, the message thread that corrects what was agreed, the work repeated because half the room was not listening. None of it is scheduled, none of it is priced, and all of it is paid for in the same currency. A meeting that produces no decision does not end when people leave the room. It keeps charging.

Why meetings multiply

In 1955, C. Northcote Parkinson observed that work expands to fill the time available for its completion. Meetings obey the same law: a meeting given an hour will take an hour, whatever it actually needed. And because every meeting feels costless, there is no natural limit on how many of them appear.

The numbers show how far the habit has gone. Writing in the Harvard Business Review in 2017, Leslie Perlow and her colleagues reported that executives spend an average of nearly 23 hours a week in meetings — up from less than 10 hours a week in the 1960s. That is 57.5% of a 40-hour week, or 1,196 hours a year; at $60 an hour, it is $71,760 of executive time spent sitting in rooms. In their survey of 182 senior managers, 71% called meetings unproductive and inefficient, 65% said meetings kept them from completing their own work, and 64% said meetings came at the expense of deep thinking. Microsoft’s 2022 Work Trend Index found that weekly meeting time had risen 252% since February 2020. The calendar did not fill itself. It filled one unpriced invitation at a time.

Five rules for meetings that earn their price

A meeting is not the enemy. Some decisions genuinely need people in a room together. The question is whether each meeting earns what it costs — and five rules make the answer honest.

1. No decision, no meeting. Every invitation should name the decision it exists to make and the person who owns it. If there is no decision, the meeting is a message wearing a calendar invite. Send the message.

2. Shorten the default. A one-hour meeting is a habit, not a requirement. Cut the eight-person meeting to 30 minutes and it costs $120 instead of $240 — a saving of $6,240 a year from a single change. Use 25- and 50-minute defaults, and let the leftover minutes be the buffer people actually need.

3. Written first, meeting second. Status updates, background reading and simple approvals belong in a document, not a room. A meeting should start where the document ends — with the disagreement, the trade-off, or the decision that only a conversation can resolve.

4. Put the price on the invitation. Add the cost to the invite itself: eight people, one hour, $240. When the price is visible, the guest list shrinks on its own. Every extra person is no longer a courtesy; they are a line item, and most of them will happily be excused.

5. Audit the calendar every quarter. List every recurring meeting, its cost, and what it produced in the last month. Cancel anything that cannot point to a decision it made. A calendar, like a budget, only stays honest if someone reviews it.

Look at your calendar for this week and ask the question a budget asks of every line: what did this buy? If a meeting cannot answer that, it is not a meeting. It is a habit — and habits are the most expensive item on any agenda.

Key takeaways

  • One weekly hour with eight people at $30 an hour costs $240 a meeting and $12,480 a year.
  • Three ordinary recurring meetings can cost $50,830 a year — roughly another full-time salary.
  • Interrupted work takes an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to resume (Gloria Mark, UC Irvine).
  • Executives average nearly 23 hours a week in meetings — 57.5% of a 40-hour week (Harvard Business Review, 2017).
  • In HBR’s survey of 182 senior managers, 71% called meetings unproductive and inefficient.
  • Meetings that earn their price have a decision, an owner, a 25- or 50-minute limit, and a quarterly audit.

Sources

  • Leslie A. Perlow, Constance Noonan Hadley, and Eunice Eun, “Stop the Meeting Madness,” Harvard Business Review, July–August 2017 — executives average nearly 23 hours a week in meetings, up from less than 10 in the 1960s; survey of 182 senior managers.
  • Gloria Mark, Daniel Gudith, and Ulrich Klocke, “The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress,” Proceedings of CHI 2008 — interrupted work takes an average of 23 minutes and 15 seconds to resume.
  • Microsoft, “Great Expectations: Making Hybrid Work Work,” Work Trend Index Annual Report 2022 — weekly meeting time up 252% since February 2020.
  • C. Northcote Parkinson, “Parkinson’s Law,” The Economist, 19 November 1955 — work expands to fill the time available for its completion.

articles.title: The Strongest Sentence a Leader Can Say
articles.excerpt: Three words long, it costs nothing, and it is the hardest sentence in management: “I was wrong.” Admitting a mistake does not make a leader look weak — it gives everyone else permission to tell the truth, while things are still cheap to fix.
articles.body_html:
There is a sentence most leaders will avoid for their entire career. Three words long, it costs nothing, and it is the hardest sentence in management: “I was wrong.” Most leaders would rather explain, deflect, or stay silent — and the team learns the real rule: here, mistakes are hidden, not fixed.

Teams that admit mistakes fastest usually make the fewest costly ones. Admitting a mistake does not make a leader look weak — it gives everyone else permission to tell the truth, while things are still cheap to fix.

All dollar figures in this article are illustrative, worked from the stated assumptions.

What Google found in 180 teams

In 2012, Google set out to build the perfect team. Over two years, its People Analytics group studied 180 teams, measuring 250 attributes — from personality types to how often teammates socialised outside work. The researchers expected the answer to be about who was on the team.

None of it mattered. No mix of talent, seniority, or background predicted success. What mattered was how the team worked together. Five dynamics set the best teams apart, and one mattered far more than the rest:

RankDynamicThe question it asks
1Psychological safetyCan we take risks without feeling insecure or embarrassed?
2DependabilityCan we count on each other to do high-quality work on time?
3Structure and clarityDo we know our goals, our roles, and our plans?
4MeaningDoes the work matter to us personally?
5ImpactDo we believe our work makes a difference?

Google called psychological safety “by far the most important” of the five: the shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking — asking, disagreeing, admitting a mistake — without being embarrassed or punished. The other four depend on it.

A team’s journey is measured in trust, not miles — every honest admission moves the whole group forward.

The hospital paradox

Long before Google, a Harvard researcher found the same truth from the opposite direction. In the mid-1990s, Amy Edmondson studied medication errors in hospital nursing units, expecting the best-led teams to make the fewest. The data said the opposite: the best-rated teams reported more errors, not fewer.

Edmondson did not conclude that good teams made more mistakes, but that they reported more of the ones they made. Where reporting an error was routine work, errors surfaced; where it meant personal exposure, they stayed hidden. The teams with the fewest logged errors were not the safest — they were the teams where mistakes went unmentioned and unlearned from. She formalised the idea in 1999, in a study of 51 work teams, naming it psychological safety: “a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking.”

What silence costs

Silence is not free. A mistake caught early is a conversation; caught late, it is a crisis. Take a small error in a proposal — a wrong price, a wrong date. The figures below are an illustration, assuming eight people at about $30 an hour each.

When the mistake is foundWhat it takes to fixIllustrative cost
In the draft, by the person who made it1 person, 30 minutesabout $15
In the team review meeting8 people, 1 hourabout $240
After it reaches the client8 people, 4 hours of reworkabout $960

Found one step later, the same mistake costs sixteen times as much — $240 instead of $15. Found after it reaches the client, sixty-four times as much — $960, plus the apology, plus the trust. Saying “I was wrong” early buys the mistake at its cheapest price.

What to do this week

Safety is not built with a speech, but with small, repeated proof that honesty is safe here. Five moves for this week:

  1. 1. Say it first. Next time you get something wrong, say so in front of the team: “I was wrong about this, and here is what I learned.” The leader goes first, or nobody goes at all.
  2. 2. Thank the messenger. When someone brings bad news, thank them first — if anger greets bad news, the next piece arrives late, or never.
  3. 3. Ask what we missed. End meetings with one question — “What are we not seeing?” — then wait. That silence is people deciding whether it is safe to speak.
  4. 4. Review the mistake, not the person. Ask what happened and what will change — never who is to blame. A blameless review turns an error into a lesson everyone keeps.
  5. 5. Count the voices. In your next meeting, notice who speaks and who does not — and invite the quiet ones in by name.

The sentence that builds the team

A leader’s authority comes not from never being wrong, but from being trusted — and trust is built when honesty would be easier to avoid. “I was wrong” is a team learning out loud.

The strongest teams are not the ones with the fewest mistakes, but the ones where mistakes are found fastest and never repeated twice. It starts with one sentence, said by one person, in front of everyone. When did you last say it — and what would change if you said it this week?

Key takeaways

  • “I was wrong” is the hardest sentence in management — and the one that builds the most trust.
  • Google’s Project Aristotle (180 teams, 250 attributes) found psychological safety “by far the most important” of five dynamics.
  • The five dynamics, in order: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, impact.
  • In Edmondson’s hospital study, the best teams reported more errors — because they felt safe enough to talk about them.
  • A mistake found in the draft costs about $15; after it reaches the client, about $960 — 64 times more.
  • Build safety this week: say it first, thank the messenger, ask what was missed, review the mistake not the person, count the voices.

Sources

  • Charles Duhigg, “What Google Learned From Its Quest to Build the Perfect Team,” The New York Times, 25 February 2016 — Project Aristotle: 180 teams, 250 attributes, psychological safety “by far the most important”.
  • Amy C. Edmondson, “Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams,” Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2), 1999, pp. 350–383 — the 51-team study and the definition.
  • re:Work — Amy Edmondson: Psychological Safety and Fearless Teams — the hospital study: the best teams reported more errors.

Note: the cost table is an illustration from the stated assumptions ($30 an hour, eight people).

articles.title: Debit or Credit? Know Which Card to Reach For
articles.excerpt: A debit card spends money you already have. A credit card spends the bank's money — and if you do not pay it back in full, the bank charges you about 22% a year for the privilege. Same plastic, opposite rules.
articles.body_html:
Hold a debit card and a credit card side by side and they look identical: the same size, the same chip, the same tap. But they are opposites. One spends money you already own. The other spends money you do not own yet — and charges you for the delay. The card you reach for is a decision, not a habit.

All figures in this article are in US dollars.

Two cards, two kinds of money

When you pay with a debit card, the money leaves your bank account within a day or two. The purchase is finished the moment it clears: nothing to repay, no interest to pay. Your spending is limited by your balance — its weakness and its strength.

A credit card works the other way round. The bank pays the shop, and you owe the bank. Each month you receive a statement, and you have a grace period — at least 21 days by law in the United States — to pay the full balance with no interest at all. Pay in full, every month, and the credit card costs you nothing: a free short-term loan, plus whatever rewards the card offers. Pay less, and the deal changes completely: whatever you leave unpaid starts earning interest, and credit card interest is among the most expensive borrowing in everyday life.

Same plastic, opposite rules — one card spends your money, the other spends the bank's.

What credit really costs

According to the Federal Reserve, the average annual interest rate on credit card accounts that were actually charged interest is about 22%. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau found that the average rate almost doubled in a decade, from 12.9% in late 2013 to 22.8% in 2023 — the highest since the Federal Reserve began collecting this data in 1994.

At 20% a year, $1,000 left unpaid costs about $200 in interest over twelve months. The average card balance is around $6,600 — at 21%, that is about $1,386 a year in interest alone, money that buys nothing and builds nothing. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York reported balances of $1.28 trillion in the fourth quarter of 2025, a new record. Late fees, annual fees, and cash advances — interest from day one, no grace period — add to the bill.

The minimum-payment trap

Every statement offers a minimum payment — usually 2% of the balance or $25, whichever is higher. It sounds like a kindness. It is the most expensive option on the page. Take a $1,000 purchase at 20%:

How you payTime to clear itInterest paidTotal paid
Minimum onlyabout 5½ yearsabout $662$1,662
$50 a month25 monthsabout $227$1,227
$100 a month12 monthsabout $103$1,103

Same $1,000 purchase: $1,662 on the minimum, $1,103 at $100 a month. The $559 difference is the price of paying slowly — the minimum is designed to keep the account open, not to get you out of debt.

When each card wins

Credit wins when you pay in full every month. Then it is a free loan that builds your credit history, usually carries stronger fraud protection, and is safer for travel and online shopping — a disputed charge is the bank's money while it is investigated, not yours.

Debit wins everywhere else: everyday spending, because you can only spend what you have; tight months, because it cannot create a debt; and any month you are not sure you can pay in full — because the moment you carry a balance, every reward point is wiped out many times over by the interest. One honest rule: if you cannot pay the full balance this month, you cannot afford the purchase on credit. Use the debit card — or wait.

What to do this week

  1. 1. Find your APR on your statement. If it is above 20%, that card is for paying in full only — never for carrying a balance.
  2. 2. Set up autopay for the full statement balance. This one setting turns a credit card from a debt trap into a free tool.
  3. 3. If you carry a balance today, stop using that card for new purchases and pay a fixed amount every month — not the minimum.
  4. 4. Make the debit card your daily default and the credit card your deliberate choice: credit when you will pay in full, debit for everything else.

The card is a tool; the habit is the decision

Neither card is good or bad on its own. A debit card cannot trap you in debt, but it cannot build your credit history either. A credit card can be a free loan with rewards, or the most expensive money you will ever borrow — the difference is entirely in how you use it. The question is never which one is better, but which one this purchase deserves. Next time you reach for your wallet, ask: whose money am I spending — mine, or the bank's?

Key takeaways

  • A debit card spends money you already have; a credit card spends the bank's money — and charges about 22% a year on what you do not repay in full.
  • Pay the full balance inside the grace period (at least 21 days) and the credit card costs nothing.
  • $1,000 left unpaid at 20% costs about $200 a year; the average balance of about $6,600 costs about $1,386 a year.
  • On a $1,000 balance at 20%, the minimum takes about 5½ years and about $662 in interest; $100 a month clears it in 12 months for about $103.
  • Credit wins when you pay in full; debit wins for everyday spending and whenever you might carry a balance.

Sources

  • Federal Reserve, G.19 Consumer Credit — average APR on accounts assessed interest, about 22%.
  • Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — average APR rose from 12.9% in late 2013 to 22.8% in 2023, the highest since the Federal Reserve began collecting the data.
  • Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Household Debt and Credit — credit card balances reached $1.28 trillion in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Note: the 21-day grace period is the minimum under the CARD Act of 2009 in the United States; the average balance of about $6,600 is from TransUnion; all tables are arithmetic from the stated assumptions.

articles.title: The Magic of Compound Interest
articles.excerpt: Put $100 in a jar every month and after 30 years you will have $36,000. Invest that same $100 every month at 7% a year, and you will have about $122,000 — the difference is time doing its quiet work.
articles.body_html:
Put $100 in a jar every month, and after 30 years you will have $36,000. Put that same $100 every month into something that earns an average of 7% a year, and after 30 years you will have about $122,000. The money you put in is identical. The difference — about $86,000 — is time doing its quiet work.

All figures in this article are in US dollars.

What compound interest really means

Simple interest pays you only on the money you put in. Compound interest pays you on the money you put in — and on the interest you have already earned. Each year, your earnings start earning their own earnings. The growth feeds on itself, so the curve bends upward: slow at first, then steeper and steeper.

At first the effect is almost invisible. In the first year, $100 a month at 7% earns only about $84. Nothing to celebrate. But by year 20, the same habit is earning more than $3,600 a year in growth alone — three times what you put in that year. The money has started working harder than you do.

Small amounts, given time, become big — the curve of $100 a month at 7% bends upward as the years pass.

The three ingredients

Three things decide how big the snowball gets: how much you put in, the return you earn, and how long you let it roll. Of the three, the one people underestimate most is time. Look at what $100 a month, invested at an average return of 7% a year, becomes:

AfterYou put inIt grows to
10 years$12,000about $17,308
20 years$24,000about $52,093
30 years$36,000about $121,997

After 10 years, your money has grown by less than half. After 30 years, it has more than tripled — and about $86,000 of the final amount, more than two-thirds of it, is growth you never deposited. That is compounding: the longer the runway, the more the growth does the heavy lifting.

Double the amount and the result doubles: $200 a month at the same 7% becomes about $243,994 in 30 years. But doubling the time does far more than doubling the amount — which brings us to the real lesson.

Time beats money

Two people, same habit, same return. One starts at 25, the other at 35. Both invest $100 a month until they are 65:

Starts atYou put inAt 65 you have
25$48,000about $262,481
35$36,000about $121,997

The early starter put in only $12,000 more — but ends up with about $140,000 more. Ten extra years at the beginning more than doubled the result. The first ten years are worth more than the last ten, because early money has the most time to compound.

This is why “I will start when I earn more” is the most expensive sentence in personal finance. Waiting ten years does not cost you ten years of contributions — it costs you the most powerful ten years of growth.

The Rule of 72

Want a quick estimate of how fast money doubles? Divide 72 by the annual return. At 7%, your money doubles roughly every 10 years. At 10%, every 7.2 years. At 3% — the kind of rate a savings account might pay — it takes 24 years.

The rule works in reverse too: at 5% inflation, prices double in about 14 years — so money left standing still loses half its buying power in that time. The same force builds your wealth when you invest, and quietly takes it away when you do not.

What to do this week

You do not need a large sum. You need four small steps:

  1. 1. Pick a number you will not miss. Start with $50 or $100 a month — an amount small enough that you will keep it up even in a tight month.
  2. 2. Automate it. Set the transfer for the day your salary arrives, so the money is invested before you can spend it.
  3. 3. Choose something boring and broad. For most people, that means a low-cost index fund that tracks the whole market, held for years, not days. You do not need to pick winners. You need patience.
  4. 4. Leave it alone. Check once a year, adjust the amount if you can, and ignore the daily noise. Consistency beats cleverness.

Start before you feel ready

Compound interest rewards the starter, not the waiter. Nobody feels ready — the amount always feels too small, the moment never feels right. But every year you wait is a year your money cannot compound.

The best time to start was ten years ago. The second-best time is today. What will your $100 a month be doing while you sleep — growing, or standing still?

Key takeaways

  • Compound interest earns returns on your returns — growth feeds on itself, so the curve bends upward over time.
  • $100 a month at 7% grows to about $17,308 in 10 years, $52,093 in 20 years, and $121,997 in 30 years.
  • About $86,000 of that $121,997 is growth — more than two-thirds of the final amount.
  • Starting at 25 instead of 35 adds about $140,000 by age 65, for only $12,000 more in contributions.
  • The Rule of 72: divide 72 by the annual return to find how many years it takes money to double.
  • Automate a small monthly amount into a low-cost, diversified investment — and leave it alone.

Sources

  • S&P Dow Jones Indices — S&P 500 historical returns data (long-run average total return of about 10% per year nominal, about 7% after adjusting for inflation).
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern School of Business — Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills (annual dataset, 1928–present).
  • Investopedia — Average Annual Return for the S&P 500 (about 10.56% nominal and 6.69% inflation-adjusted since 1957).

Note: the 7% figure is an illustrative long-run average from the sources above; all tables are arithmetic from the stated assumptions. The Rule of 72 is a standard approximation.

articles.title: Your Money Is Quietly Losing Value
articles.excerpt: Most people think saving means watching the number stay the same. But that number is lying — inflation quietly shrinks what your money can buy, every single year.
articles.body_html:
Most people think saving money means keeping it in the bank and watching the number stay the same. But that number is lying to you.

All figures in this article are in US dollars.

The silent tax

If inflation is 5% a year and your savings earn 1%, your money loses 4% of its buying power every year. After 10 years, $10,000 in savings buys what about $6,650 buys today. You didn't spend a thing — and you still got poorer.

This is not a one-off loss. It compounds, year after year, silently. Here is what happens to $10,000 left sitting in a savings account at a 4% real loss per year:

After$10,000 is worth
5 yearsabout $8,150
10 yearsabout $6,650
20 yearsabout $4,420
30 yearsabout $2,940

After 30 years, more than two-thirds of your money's value is gone — without you spending a single coin. That is the silent tax.

Growth vs. standing still — money that grows keeps pace with rising prices; money that stands still falls behind them.

Why your salary feels smaller every year

The same force shrinks your income. If your salary rises 2% in a year but prices rise 5%, you did not get a raise — you took a 3% pay cut in real terms. Your bank balance went up, but your life got more expensive faster. This is why so many people feel they are working harder yet falling behind: the numbers on the payslip grow, but what those numbers buy shrinks.

The lesson is simple: a number that does not grow faster than prices is a number going backwards — whether it is your salary or your savings.

Saving and growing are two different jobs

Saving protects you from emergencies. Growing protects you from inflation. You need both: an emergency fund for safety, and investments — even small, regular ones — for growth.

Your emergency fund comes first: 3–6 months of expenses, kept in an accessible savings account. Only after that safety net is in place should extra money go to work.

Growing your money does not mean gambling on risky bets. It means putting your money where it earns more than inflation over the long run — for most people, that means a low-cost index fund that tracks the whole market, held for years, not days. You do not need to pick winners. You need patience.

The power of starting early

Time is the ingredient most people underestimate. Look at what happens when you invest just $50 a month in a low-cost index fund earning an average of 7% a year:

AfterYou put inIt grows to
10 years$6,000about $8,650
20 years$12,000about $26,000
30 years$18,000about $61,000

After 30 years, your money has more than tripled — and two-thirds of that growth came from time and compounding, not from what you put in. The best time to start was ten years ago. The second-best time is today.

What to do this week

You do not need a perfect plan. You need four small steps:

  1. 1. Check your savings rate. Find out what your bank actually pays you — then compare it to inflation. If the gap is wide, your money is shrinking.
  2. 2. Build your emergency fund. Start with one month of expenses, then grow it to three, then six.
  3. 3. Automate a small monthly investment. Even $50 a month, invested automatically the day your salary arrives, so you never have to think about it.
  4. 4. Review once a year. Check your numbers, adjust the amount if you can, and leave the rest alone. Consistency beats cleverness.

Start small, start now

Even $50 a month in a low-cost index fund, done consistently for years, beats a savings account standing still. The amount matters less than the habit — and the earlier you start, the more time works for you instead of against you.

The question is not whether you can afford to invest. It is whether you can afford not to. What does your money do while you sleep — grow, or shrink?

Key takeaways

  • Inflation at 5% with 1% savings interest means a 4% real loss every year.
  • $10,000 left idle is worth about $6,650 in 10 years — and about $2,940 in 30.
  • A 2% raise against 5% inflation is a 3% pay cut in real terms.
  • Keep an emergency fund of 3–6 months of expenses first.
  • $50 a month at 7% grows to about $26,000 in 20 years and $61,000 in 30.
  • Invest small amounts regularly — consistency beats size.

Sources

  • S&P Dow Jones Indices — S&P 500 historical returns data (long-run average total return of about 10% per year nominal, about 7% after adjusting for inflation).
  • Aswath Damodaran, NYU Stern School of Business — Historical Returns on Stocks, Bonds and Bills (annual dataset, 1928–present).
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index (CPI) data, the standard measure of U.S. inflation.
  • Investopedia — Average Annual Return for the S&P 500 (about 10.56% nominal and 6.69% inflation-adjusted since 1957).

Note: the 5% inflation and 1% savings figures in this article are an illustrative example; the 7% long-run return figure comes from the sources above. All tables are arithmetic worked from those stated assumptions.
